headline: Schema validation costs the size of the schema and the value, not the number of paths through them
summary: Four validators and one schema converter walked every path through a schema or a value, so an input of linear size could cost exponential time. The most exposed was `b.safeSchema`, which `b.router` runs on every request body: an expression-tree schema built from a `union` of operator objects that recurse through `lazy` took 2.5 seconds and 1.7 GB of heap on a 339-byte JSON body twelve levels deep, and wrote a 531 MB 400 response; one more level exhausts the heap. `b.jsonSchema.validate` was exponential in the same way for a schema whose definitions reach the next one twice per level and for an ordinary recursive `anyOf`/`oneOf` schema against a deeply nested value, and `uniqueItems` compared every pair of items, so a 785 KB array of 128,000 numbers took 3.2 seconds. Each validator now runs a subschema at most once per value where one can be reached by several paths, and each refuses with its own error the shapes that cannot be collapsed that way. Separately, the framework writers that set their own `Cache-Control` (`b.render`, `b.middleware.sse`, the API-document and well-known middlewares, `b.staticServe`) replaced the `no-store` that `b.middleware.noCache` had set, so an authenticated page reached the browser with a header that lets the browser store it; they now keep an earlier `no-store`. Options that keep an operator RegExp and run it on later calls now refuse the `g` and `y` flags, which made each match start where the previous request's match ended: `b.middleware.csrfProtect({ skipPaths: [/\/health/y] })` skipped the CSRF check for a POST to `/api/v1/health` sent right after a POST to `/health`. `b.middleware.sse` no longer throws on every node:http response. `b.mail.arc.evaluate` reported a message sealed with an attacker's own key as sealed by a domain in `trustedSealers` when the ARC-Seal named that domain in an earlier `d=`; it now trusts only the domain whose key verified the seal. `b.mail.dmarc.evaluate` returned `none` for mail spoofing a domain that publishes `v = DMARC1; p=reject` or `V=DMARC1; p=reject`, or a valid record beside one starting `v=DMARC10`, so that mail was not rejected; the DMARC, SPF, MTA-STS, TLS-RPT and DKIM key-record lookups now select records by the version grammar their RFCs define. `b.network.smtp.mtaSts.fetch` returned no policy as soon as the `_mta-sts` TXT answer was missing or the policy host was unreachable, so an attacker who can block those responses could turn off an `enforce` policy the sender had already cached; it now applies the cached policy until its `max_age` elapses (RFC 8461 §3.3). The control-character checks now refuse the C1 controls U+0080 to U+009F, which include U+009B, the one-character form of `ESC [`.

items.title: b.mail.arc.evaluate reports a trusted sealer only for the domain whose key verified the seal
items.body: `arc.evaluate` read each hop's sealer domain with its own pattern, the first `d=` after a delimiter in the ARC-Seal header, while `arc.verify` verified the seal with the key named by the parsed `d=` tag. A sealer holding only the key for its own domain could therefore be reported as any domain in `trustedSealers`. A message sealed and signed with `attacker.example`'s key returned `chainStatus: "pass"`, `trusted: true` and `trustedDomain: "trusted.example"` when the ARC-Seal carried `d=trusted.example` earlier in the header than its real `d=attacker.example` tag, in any of three forms: as a repeated `d=` tag, as text after the signature inside the `b=` value, or inside the value of an unknown tag. An operator that relaxes DMARC for mail sealed by a trusted intermediary accepted such a message. `arc.verify` now returns the domain it verified each seal with as `hops[].sealDomain`, and `arc.evaluate` trusts only that domain. The ARC-Seal `cv=` value is read from the same parsed tags: a seal with `cv=nonesuch` was read as `cv=none` and now fails the chain with reason `invalid-cv-at-i=<n>`.

items.title: DKIM and ARC refuse a tag-list that repeats a tag name, and a b= value that is not base64
items.body: RFC 6376 §3.2 makes a tag-list that repeats a tag name invalid as a whole. `b.mail.dkim.verify` kept the last value of a repeated tag, so a DKIM-Signature carrying `s=` or `h=` twice verified as `pass`, and a key record carrying `p=` or `k=` twice was used. Such a signature is now `permerror`, and such a key record is skipped like any other invalid record. `b.mail.arc.verify` fails a chain whose ARC-Seal or ARC-Message-Signature repeats a tag with reason `invalid-tag-list`. The signature value was decoded with a base64 reader that ignores text after the padding, so a `b=` of the signature followed by other text verified; a `b=` that is not canonical base64 is now `permerror` for DKIM and fails the ARC hop (RFC 6376 §3.5). ARC reads a hop's instance number with one reader in `arc.verify`, `arc.evaluate` and `arc.sign`, following RFC 8617 §3.9 and §4.1: the header opens with `i=` and a number followed by `;`, with folding whitespace and comments allowed around each token (`i = 1 (forwarded);`), in the ARC-Seal and ARC-Message-Signature as well as the ARC-Authentication-Results. A header whose `i=` is not first is not read as part of a hop. `arc.evaluate` takes `finalAr` from the ARC-Authentication-Results that `arc.verify` grouped for the last hop, now also returned as `hops[].authenticationResults`, and returns `null` when that instance carries two of them.

items.title: b.safeSchema validates a recursive union in time proportional to the value, and bounds the issues it reports
items.body: `union` tried every option in turn and collected every failed option's issues, and `object` kept validating keys after its first failure. For a schema like `Expr = s.union([bin("+"), bin("-"), bin("*"), s.number()])` with operands that recurse through `s.lazy`, a value that fails at its deepest leaf was validated options^depth times and returned options^depth issues. Through `b.router`'s `{ body: schema }` validation, a 339-byte body twelve levels deep took 2.5 seconds and wrote a 531 MB 400 response. A `union` evaluated inside another union's option now checks each option's literal, enum, string, number and boolean keys first and stops the option at its first failure, for objects, arrays, tuples and records whose schema holds no `refine`, `transform` or `preprocess` callback, no `default` or `catch` factory and no unresolved `lazy`; those are still validated field by field in order. While a `union` or a `lazy` target is being validated, a schema that already failed for a value is not run again for that value: the earlier failure is reported at the new position, and each of its issues counts toward the evaluation limit below. A schema that already accepted a value at the same position returns that result again. A result is reused only when no `refine`, `transform` or `preprocess` callback, `lazy` getter, or `default` or `catch` factory ran while it was computed or has run since. This shape now costs the size of the body, including the first parse with a newly built schema whose `lazy` references are not yet resolved, and a `transform` or a `default` factory still runs for every value it produces. A failed `union` reports its summary issue, the first 100 issues its options reported, and one `union/issues-omitted` issue with the count it left out; a nested union reports only the first failure of each of its options. A value built in code that reuses one object at every level of a recursive schema is refused with `safe-schema/evaluation-limit` (from `safeParse` as the only error, from `parse` as the thrown `SafeSchemaError`) once validation passes 100,000 checks and 1,000 checks per node of the value.

items.title: b.jsonSchema.validate no longer walks every path through reference diamonds and recursive alternatives
items.body: A schema whose `$defs` each reach the next definition twice (through `allOf`, `anyOf`, `oneOf`, `if`/`then`/`else`, `not`, a `$ref` beside another applicator, `dependentSchemas`, `unevaluatedProperties`, or `$dynamicRef`) cost 2^depth evaluations: a 24-level schema of about 2 KB took 6.3 seconds to validate the string `"aaa"`. An ordinary recursive schema whose alternatives descend into the same child, such as an expression tree, cost branches^depth on a value a few hundred bytes long. Validation now remembers the result of a `$ref` target referenced from more than one place, and of every `$dynamicRef` target, for each value and dynamic scope, so these shapes cost the size of the schema and the value. The errors reported are unchanged, including their order and the `maxErrors` cut-off. A shape that still reaches the same subschema and value through more paths than its size accounts for, such as a value built in code that reuses one array at every level, is refused with `json-schema/evaluation-limit` once validation passes 100,000 evaluations and four times the schema's positions multiplied by the value's size.

items.title: Framework responses keep a Cache-Control no-store that is already on the response
items.body: `b.middleware.noCache` sets `Cache-Control: no-store` on authenticated and individualized responses, and the framework writers that ran after it replaced the header with their own default. A page sent through `b.render` behind `noCache` reached the browser with `private, no-cache, must-revalidate`, which lets the browser's own cache store the page (RFC 9111 §5.2.2.4); `no-store` forbids storing it (§5.2.2.5). The same replacement happened in `b.render.json`, `text`, `htmlString`, `redirect`, `stream` and `create().html` (`private, no-cache, must-revalidate`); `b.middleware.sse` and `b.sse.create` (`no-cache, no-transform`); the JMAP EventSource handler (`no-cache`); `b.middleware.openapiServe`, `b.middleware.asyncapiServe` and `b.openapi.create().middleware` (`public, max-age=300` or their `cacheControl` option); `b.middleware.securityTxt`, `assetlinks` and `webAppManifest` (`public, max-age=86400`); `b.middleware.protectedResourceMetadata` (`public, max-age=3600`); `b.a2a.middleware.agentCard` (`public, max-age=300`); and `b.staticServe` and `b.router.serveStatic` (their file cache policy, including on 304 responses). Each now sends the `Cache-Control` already on the response when it carries `no-store`, adding `no-transform` where its own default has that directive. A `Cache-Control` the caller passes in `opts.headers` does not remove it either: keep a route that must stay cacheable out of the middleware's scope with `b.middleware.noCache({ when })`. The rule is available as `b.cdnCacheControl.keepNoStore(res, fallback)` and as `b.requestHelpers.finalizeHeaders(res, headers)`, which applies it after merging caller headers and merges `Vary`.

items.title: Framework responses keep a Vary that is already on the response
items.body: A middleware that makes the response depend on a request header adds that header to `Vary` with `setHeader`: `b.middleware.cors` adds `Origin` and `b.middleware.compression` adds `Accept-Encoding`. node:http lets a header object passed to `res.writeHead` replace a header set that way, so a writer that sent its own `Vary` dropped the earlier tokens, and a shared cache could store one response for every value of the dropped header. `b.render.json`, `text`, `htmlString`, `redirect` and `stream` sent only the `Vary` in `opts.headers`; a response with `Vary: Cookie` already set and `opts.headers: { Vary: "Accept-Language" }` went out as `Vary: Accept-Language`. `b.middleware.sse` sent only a `Vary` in its `headers` option, `b.middleware.openapiServe` and `b.middleware.asyncapiServe` replaced `Vary` with `Origin` when `accessControl.allowOrigin` is set, `b.middleware.noCache` replaced it with its `vary` option, and `b.middleware.compression` appended `Accept-Encoding` to the header object a handler passed to `writeHead` without the `Vary` already on the response. Each now sends the earlier tokens followed by its own, each once. The merge is available as `b.requestHelpers.mergeVary(res, headers)`.

items.title: Options that keep an operator RegExp and run it on later calls refuse the g and y flags
items.body: A RegExp with the `g` or `y` flag starts each `test()` at the `lastIndex` the previous call left, so a pattern stored in configuration gave answers that depended on the request, row or file before. `b.safeSchema.string().regex(/^alice$/g)` accepted `"alice"` on every second parse. `b.guardCsv.schema` with a `/^[a-z]+$/g` column refused the second of three matching rows. `b.middleware.csrfProtect({ skipPaths: [/\/health/y] })` refused a POST to `/api/v1/health` with 403, and skipped the CSRF check for the same POST sent right after a POST to `/health`; `skipPaths` on `b.middleware.fetchMetadata`, `b.middleware.rateLimit` and `b.middleware.botGuard` is matched the same way. These options now throw when they are given a RegExp with either flag: `b.middleware.botGuard` `allowedAgents`, `blockedAgents` (`bot-guard/stateful-pattern`); `skipPaths` on `csrfProtect`, `fetchMetadata`, `rateLimit`, `botGuard` and `b.requestHelpers.makeSkipMatcher`, and `b.middleware.requestLog` `skipPaths` (`regex/stateful-pattern`); `b.middleware.spanHttpServer` `ignorePaths` (`span-http/stateful-pattern`); `b.middleware.requestId` `formatRegex` (`request-id/stateful-pattern`); `b.middleware.cors` `origins` (`cors/stateful-pattern`, as before); `b.staticServe.create` `hashedPathPattern` (`static/stateful-pattern`); `b.safeSql.validateIdentifier` `pattern` (`sql/stateful-pattern`); `b.safeSchema.string().regex` (`safe-schema/stateful-pattern`); `b.guardCsv.schema` column `regex` (`csv.stateful-pattern`); `b.mail.helo.evaluate` `genericRdnsPatterns` (`mail-helo/stateful-pattern`); `b.selfUpdate.poll` `assetPattern` and `signaturePattern` (`selfupdate/stateful-asset-pattern`, `selfupdate/stateful-sig-pattern`); `b.dev.create` `ignore` (`dev/stateful-pattern`); and `b.parsers.env.parse` `keyShape` (`env/stateful-pattern`). The check is available as `b.guardRegex.assertStateless(input, label?, ErrorClass?, code?)`. `skipPaths` and `ignorePaths` are copied when the middleware is created, so an entry added to the caller's array afterwards is not matched.

items.title: Operator patterns run against request data are screened for ReDoS
items.body: Five options ran an operator RegExp without `b.guardRegex.assertSafe`: `b.safeSchema.string().regex` (run on request bodies through `b.router`), `b.guardCsv.schema` column `regex`, `b.middleware.requestId` `formatRegex` (run on the inbound request-id header), `b.parsers.env.parse` `keyShape`, and a RegExp `sep` passed to `b.structuredFields.parseTagList`. Each now screens the pattern and throws `safe-schema/unsafe-pattern`, `csv.unsafe-pattern`, `request-id/unsafe-pattern`, `env/unsafe-pattern` or `regex/unsafe-pattern` for a shape the screen refuses.

items.title: b.mail.dmarc.evaluate reads a DMARC record whose version tag has spaces or an uppercase V
items.body: RFC 9989 defines the DMARC version tag as `"v" *WSP "=" *WSP %s"DMARC1"`: the tag name is case-insensitive and whitespace may surround the `=`. The record lookup kept only TXT records that began with the exact characters `v=DMARC1`. For a domain publishing `v = DMARC1; p=reject` or `V=DMARC1; p=reject`, `evaluate` returned `result: "none"` for mail that failed SPF and DKIM alignment, and a domain publishing `v=DMARC1; p=reject` beside a second record starting `v=DMARC10` also returned `none`. All three now return `fail` with `p=reject`. A record starting `v=DMARC10` or `v=DMARC1x` is not a DMARC record: as the only record it returned `permerror` and now returns `none`. `b.mail.dmarc.parseRecord` refuses a record whose version tag does not match the grammar.

items.title: b.network.smtp.mtaSts.fetch applies a cached policy when no live policy is available
items.body: `fetch` resolved the `_mta-sts` TXT record before it consulted its cache, and returned `null` when the record was missing, malformed or could not be resolved. When the TXT `id` changed and the policy host was unreachable, answered 404, answered another non-2xx status or served a policy that did not parse, `fetch` returned `null` or threw `smtp/mta-sts-fetch-failed`. An attacker able to block DNS or HTTPS responses for a recipient domain could therefore turn off an `enforce` policy that `b.mail.send.deliver` had already cached. RFC 8461 §3.3 requires a sender to apply a valid cached policy in each of those cases, and `fetch` now returns the cached policy; with no cached policy it returns `null` or throws as before. The policy was also cached for 60 minutes whatever its `max_age`. A cached policy is now used until its `max_age` elapses, for at most 52 weeks, or for 60 minutes when the policy has no `max_age`. A TXT `id` equal to the cached policy's `id` returns the cached policy without an HTTPS request, and a fetch that failed for a new `id` is not retried for 60 minutes. The returned policy no longer carries the internal `_cacheTtlMs` field.

items.title: SPF, MTA-STS, TLS-RPT and DKIM key records are selected by their RFC version grammar
items.body: `b.mail.spf.verify` treated a TXT record starting `v=spf10` or `v=spf1x` as an SPF record: `v=spf10 +all` on its own returned `pass`, and `v=spf1 -all` published beside it returned `permerror`. RFC 7208 §4.5 ends the version section at a space or the end of the record, so those records are now ignored (the two examples return `none` and `fail`), and `b.mail.spf.parseRecord` refuses them. `b.network.smtp.mtaSts.fetch` fetched the HTTPS policy for a TXT answer that carried `v=STSv1` anywhere in a record, started `v=STSv10`, had no `id`, had an `id` longer than 32 characters, or held two `v=STSv1` records; RFC 8461 §3.1 treats each as no policy, and `fetch` now returns `null` for them unless it holds a cached policy for the domain. `b.network.smtp.tlsRpt.fetchPolicy` accepted records starting `V=TLSRPTV1`, `v=TLSRPTv1-x` or `v=TLSRPTv1.5` and used the first of two `v=TLSRPTv1` records; each now returns `null` (RFC 8460 §3). `b.mail.dkim.verify` and the key lookup in `b.mail.arc.verify` used the first TXT record at the selector that started `v=DKIM1` or contained `p=`, so a key record starting `v=DKIM2` or `v=DKIM10`, or one whose `v=` tag was not the first tag, verified signatures. RFC 6376 §3.6.1 requires `v=` to be absent or to be the first tag with the value `DKIM1`. Other records are now skipped, the first remaining record that has `p=` is used, and a signature whose selector has no remaining record gets `permerror`. The check is available as `b.structuredFields.recordVersionMatches(record, name, value, grammar)`.

items.title: Control-character checks refuse the C1 controls U+0080 to U+009F
items.body: U+009B is the one-character form of `ESC [` and starts a terminal escape sequence, and U+0085 NEXT LINE is a line break under Unicode line breaking. The shared control-character checks covered only C0 and DEL: `b.guardText` under `balanced` answered `ok: true` for text carrying either character and `sanitize` kept both, and `b.codepointClass.isForbiddenControlChar(0x9b)` returned `false`. `b.codepointClass.CTRL_RANGES`, which the text guards read for `controlPolicy`, and `isForbiddenControlChar` and `firstControlCharOffset` now include the C1 block, which is also exported as `C1_CTRL_RANGES`. The C1 controls are now refused by `b.guardText`, `b.guardFilename` (`filename.control`), `b.guardCsv`, `b.guardSql` quoted identifiers, `b.guardJwt.kidSafe`, `b.guardMessageId`, `b.guardMailCompose` header values, `b.guardMailMove` folder names, `b.guardMailSieve` names and scripts, `b.guardIdempotencyKey`, `b.guardDsn.parse`, `b.guardListId`, `b.guardListUnsubscribe`, the SMTP, IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve command guards and the mail servers that run them, `b.safeIcal`, `b.safeVcard`, `b.safeMime` header values, `b.safeJsonPath.validateKey`, `b.inbox` message ids, `b.storage.chunkScratch` assembly ids, `b.auth.stepUp.buildChallenge`, `b.middleware.bearerAuth` realms, `b.mail.feedbackId`, `b.mail.spamScore` reasons, `b.mail.deploy` domains, JMAP URLs and email addresses, and `b.localHttp` request paths. `b.safeRedirect.resolve` returns its fallback, `b.requestHelpers.extractBearer` returns `null`, `b.ai.input.classify` counts the character in `ctrlCount`, and `b.guardMarkdown` removes it from link targets. `b.structuredFields.refuseControlBytes` and `containsControlBytes` still accept 0x80 to 0x9F, because Node exposes an HTTP field value as a latin1 string in which those codes are UTF-8 continuation bytes, and `b.parsers.toml` still accepts C1 in strings, as TOML 1.0 allows; both pass the new `allowC1` option.

items.title: b.auth.fidoMds3.fetch stops serving a cached BLOB after its nextUpdate
items.body: `fetch` passed the time until the BLOB's `nextUpdate` to the cache as a bare number, which the cache ignored, so every fetched BLOB was cached for 30 days. A call made after `nextUpdate` returned the cached BLOB, with the authenticator status reports it held when it was fetched, instead of downloading the replacement. The BLOB is now cached until its `nextUpdate`, and for at most 30 days, and a cached BLOB whose `nextUpdate` has passed is fetched again.

items.title: b.jsonSchema uniqueItems runs in linear time
items.body: `uniqueItems: true` compared every pair of items, so an array of 128,000 distinct numbers (785 KB) took 3.2 seconds and an array of 32,000 small objects took 9.3 seconds. Each item is now reduced to an identifier that is equal for exactly the pairs `enum` and `const` treat as equal, so the check costs the size of the array. The error still names the first duplicate pair, `(indices i, j)`, with the lowest first index.

items.title: b.jsonSchema enum and const equality is symmetric
items.body: Object equality compared the enumerable keys of one side with the own keys of the other, so an object with a non-enumerable own property could equal a second object while the second did not equal the first. Both sides now compare enumerable own keys, which is also the equality `uniqueItems` uses.

items.title: b.jtd checks a schema object reused at several positions once
items.body: A schema built in code that reuses one object at several positions was checked once per path before any value was validated, doubling per level. Each object is now checked once. A schema whose root reappears below the root is still refused with `jtd/bad-schema`, and so is a schema object graph that contains a cycle, such as `s.elements = s`, which previously overflowed the stack.

items.title: b.safeSchema catch factories run for null
items.body: `.catch(fn)` called `fn` for a value that failed validation, but for `null` it returned `fn` itself as the parsed value: `s.number().catch(function () { return 7; }).parse(null)` returned the function. It now returns `7` in both cases.

items.title: b.middleware.sse streams over a node:http response
items.body: `b.middleware.sse` added `Vary: Accept` after `writeHead` had sent the response head. node:http refuses that with `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`, so the middleware threw before writing any event. It now adds `Vary: Accept` before the head is written, next to any `Vary` an earlier middleware set.

items.title: b.flag providers apply regex targeting rules and name themselves in result metadata
items.body: `b.flag.providers.memory`, `localFile` and `environmentVariable` validated each flag's rules but evaluated the unvalidated copy, which never carries the compiled pattern, so a rule with `op: "regex"` never matched and the flag fell back to its default. The providers now evaluate the validated rules. Their results also carried `metadata.provider: null` for every evaluation that found the flag; it is now the provider kind (`memory`, `local-file` or `environment`).

items.title: Pattern options reject a value that is not a RegExp
items.body: `b.middleware.requestId` accepted a string `formatRegex` and then threw a `TypeError` on every request that carried the request-id header; it now throws `request-id/bad-format-regex` when it is created. `b.safeSql.validateIdentifier` threw a `TypeError` for a string `pattern` and now throws `sql/bad-pattern`. `b.parsers.env.parse` ignored a `keyShape` that was not a RegExp and applied the default key shape; it now throws `env/bad-opt`. `b.mail.helo.evaluate` ignored `genericRdnsPatterns` entries that were not a RegExp and now throws `mail-helo/bad-pattern`. `b.safeSchema.string().regex` throws `safe-schema/bad-regex`, `b.guardCsv.schema` throws `csv.bad-schema` for a column that is not an object or a `regex` that is not a RegExp, and `b.dev.create` throws `dev/bad-ignore` for an `ignore` entry that is neither a RegExp nor a string.

items.title: b.guardCsv.schema copies and freezes its columns; b.auditDailyReview freezes its exported tables
items.body: `b.guardCsv.schema` kept the caller's column objects and returned them as `columns`, so changing a column's `regex` after the schema was built changed how later rows were validated without screening the new pattern. It now copies each column, and the returned `columns` array and its entries are frozen. `b.auditDailyReview.ALERT_PATTERNS`, `CRITICAL_PATTERNS`, `SEVERITY_ORDER` and `POSTURES_REQUIRING_NOTIFY` were exported as mutable arrays that the default classifier reads for every event; they and the RegExps in them are now frozen.

items.title: b.auth.jwt.verifyExternal applies jwksCacheMs
items.body: `verifyExternal` accepted `jwksCacheMs` and passed it to the cache as a bare number, which the cache ignored, so keys fetched from `jwksUri` were cached for the 10-minute default whatever the option said, and values such as `-1`, `"60000"` and `Infinity` were accepted. The option now sets how long the keys are cached (`0` does not cache them), and a value that is not a non-negative finite integer throws `auth-jwt-external/bad-jwks-cache-ms`.

items.title: b.openapi.toYaml and b.asyncapi.toYaml escape line breaks and non-printable characters
items.body: The YAML writer behind `b.openapi.toYaml`, `b.asyncapi.toYaml`, `b.middleware.openapiServe` and `b.middleware.asyncapiServe` quoted a string only when it held a YAML indicator character or leading or trailing whitespace. A key containing a line feed was written unquoted and changed the document's structure: `{ "x\ny": 1 }` read back as the string `"x"`. A value containing a carriage return made the document unparseable, and C0 controls, DEL, C1 controls, U+2028, U+2029 and U+FEFF were written unescaped, which YAML 1.2 does not allow in a stream. A string holding any of these characters is now written double-quoted, with the character written as `\n`, `\r`, `\t` or a `\u` escape.

items.title: b.openapi.schemaWalk refuses a schema it would expand without bound
items.body: `schemaWalk` copied a subschema into every position that references it, so a schema object reused at every level expanded to 2^depth nodes in the generated document, a cyclic schema overflowed the stack, and a schema nested a few thousand levels deep did the same. It now refuses with `openapi/schema-too-large` past 100,000 nodes, `openapi/schema-cycle` for a subschema that is its own ancestor, and `openapi/schema-too-deep` past 1,000 levels. A subschema used in a few places is still copied into each one.

items.title: b.cache wrap and set refuse options that are not an object
items.body: `cache.wrap(key, fn, 60000)` and `cache.set(key, value, 60000)` ignored the number and stored the entry for the instance's default `ttlMs`. Both now throw `cache/bad-opt` when the options argument is present and is not an object.

items.title: C1 controls are refused
items.body: Input carrying U+0080 to U+009F is now refused by the checks listed under Security. A caller of `b.codepointClass.isForbiddenControlChar` or `firstControlCharOffset` that scans a latin1 view of bytes, where 0x80 to 0x9F are parts of a longer UTF-8 sequence, passes `{ allowC1: true }`.

items.title: Publish one well-formed _mta-sts TXT record
items.body: Publish exactly one `_mta-sts` TXT record that starts `v=STSv1;` and carries `id=` with 1 to 32 letters and digits, the form `b.mail.deploy.mtaStsPublish` returns. A domain whose record lacks `id`, or that publishes two records, is now treated as having no MTA-STS policy by senders that have not cached one.

items.title: Scope noCache off routes that must stay cacheable
items.body: A `Cache-Control` passed in `opts.headers` to a `b.render` writer, to `b.middleware.sse`, or to an API-document middleware no longer replaces a `no-store` that `b.middleware.noCache` set on the response. A route that must remain cacheable behind that middleware is excluded from it with its predicate: `b.middleware.noCache({ when: function (req) { return req.url.indexOf("/public/") !== 0; } })`.

items.title: Pass cache options as an object
items.body: Replace a bare number passed to `cache.wrap` or `cache.set` with `{ ttlMs: <number> }`.

items.title: New refusals and a bounded union issue list
items.body: `b.jsonSchema.validate` and `isValid` can throw `json-schema/evaluation-limit`; a value built in code that reuses one array at every level of a recursive schema is refused this way. `b.safeSchema` union failures carry at most 100 option issues plus a `union/issues-omitted` issue, and `parse`/`safeParse` refuse with `safe-schema/evaluation-limit` a value that reuses one object at every level of a recursive schema. `b.openapi.schemaWalk` throws `openapi/schema-too-large`, `openapi/schema-cycle` or `openapi/schema-too-deep` for the shapes above; define a subschema used in many places once under `components/schemas` and reference it with `$ref`.

items.title: Remove the g and y flags from stored patterns
items.body: A RegExp with the `g` or `y` flag passed to any of the options listed under Security is now refused when the option is accepted. Remove the flag: `test()` matches the same values without it. A pattern that `b.guardRegex.assertSafe` refuses must be rewritten for `s.string().regex`, a `b.guardCsv.schema` column, `b.middleware.requestId` `formatRegex`, `b.parsers.env.parse` `keyShape` and a RegExp `sep` for `b.structuredFields.parseTagList`; the refusal names the shape.
